parts.title: Part 1
parts.transcript: Parroto IELTS Practice. Listening Test 20. You will hear a number of different recordings, and you will have to answer questions on what you hear. There will be time for you to read the instructions and questions, and you will have a chance to check your work. All the recordings will be played once only. The test is in four parts. Now turn to Part 1. Part 1. You will hear a woman phoning the owner of a small business that rents out campervans. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 6. Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 6. Dave: Hello, Parry's Campervans, Dave speaking. Jo: Oh, hello. I'm ringing about hiring a campervan this summer. I think you own the business with your wife, is that right? Dave: That's right. Linda and I run it together. We've got two vans at the moment. How can I help? Jo: Well, my name's Jo. Some friends of mine hired your van called Rosie last year, and they loved it. My partner and I would like to take it to Scotland for a week in July. Dave: Lovely. Which week were you thinking of? Jo: The week beginning the seventh, if possible. Dave: Let me just check. I'm sorry, Rosie's already booked that week, and the week after. It's free for the week beginning the twenty-first, though. That's actually the only week left in July. Jo: Oh. Well, I think we could manage that. I'd just need to check with work. How much would it be? Dave: July is our busiest month, so Rosie's six hundred and forty pounds for the week. Jo: Ah, that's a bit more than we were hoping to spend. We'd set ourselves a limit of about six hundred. Dave: In that case, you might like to consider our other van. It's a bit smaller, and we only finished converting it this spring. It's called Bramble. Jo: Sorry, what was the name? Dave: Bramble. That's B, R, A, M, B, L, E. Like the wild blackberry bushes. Jo: Oh, that's nice. And how much is that one? Dave: Bramble is five hundred and sixty pounds for the week, and it's free for the whole of July. Jo: That sounds better. Can you tell me a bit about it? Dave: Of course. It's got quite an unusual history, actually. It started life as an ambulance. We bought it when the ambulance service was replacing its old vehicles, and we've spent about a year converting it. So it's very solidly built. Jo: How interesting. Is it difficult to drive? I've never driven anything bigger than a small car. Dave: Not at all. It's no longer than a large family car, and it has an automatic gearbox, so most people find it very easy after the first few miles. Jo: That's a relief. And how many people does it sleep? Dave: Two, which would be perfect for you. During the day there are two comfortable seats with a table between them, and at night the seats turn into a double bed. It only takes a couple of minutes. Jo: Great. We were also hoping to do some cycling while we're away. Would there be room for our bikes? Dave: Yes, there's a rack at the back that takes two bikes. It's included in the price. Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 7 to 10. Jo: What about cooking? Is there a proper kitchen? Dave: There's a small kitchen area with a sink, a fridge and a two-ring gas stove. There isn't an oven, I'm afraid, but most people find they can cook almost anything on the stove. And we provide all the pans, plates and cutlery. Jo: That's fine. We don't need anything fancy. Is there a toilet? Dave: There's a small chemical toilet inside, but there isn't room for a shower inside the van. However, we've fitted an outdoor shower at the back, which is great for rinsing off after a day on the beach, or for washing muddy boots. Jo: That's a clever idea. Do people usually stay at campsites, or can we park anywhere? Dave: Most people use campsites, because you get electricity and proper washing facilities. We give all our customers a list of campsites that we recommend, with notes on which ones are quietest and which have the best views. Linda's visited most of them herself. Jo: Oh, that would be really helpful. And is there anything we'd need to buy, like gas? Dave: No, the gas bottle will be full when you collect the van, and so will the fuel tank. We just ask you to bring it back full. Jo: OK. Well, I think we'd like to book Bramble for the week beginning the twenty-first, please. Dave: Wonderful. We ask for a deposit of thirty per cent when you book, so that would be a hundred and sixty-eight pounds. Jo: That's fine. And when do you need the rest? Dave: Since you're coming in July, we'd need the final payment by the end of May, please. We'll send you a reminder. Jo: OK. And is insurance included in the price? Dave: Yes, the price includes full insurance for up to two drivers, and breakdown cover as well, so you won't need to arrange anything yourselves. Jo: Perfect. Shall I give you my card details now? That is the end of Part 1. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 1.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear a town councillor reporting on the town centre and on plans for a local park. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14. Chair: Right, next on the agenda is the town centre. Councillor Hale. Councillor Hale: Thank you. Well, we now have the results of the survey we carried out in the spring about the town centre. To be honest, we'd expected parking to be the biggest issue, but very few people complained about it, and the new car park behind the library seems to have helped. Some people mentioned the cost of bus fares, although that isn't something the council controls. But by far the most common concern was the growing number of empty shops. People feel that the high street is starting to look neglected, and they're worried about what that means for the town. Councillor Hale: We're looking at ways of encouraging new businesses to move in, and I'll report back on that next month. In the meantime, there are some smaller changes we can make straight away. In the market square, we'll be planting a row of trees along the south side this autumn, to provide some shade and make it a more pleasant place to sit. The fountain, which many of you will remember was broken for years, was repaired last summer and is working well. There's been talk of closing the square to cars completely, but that's a longer-term idea and it would need a lot more consultation. Councillor Hale: Now, you'll remember that we planned to put up a new bus shelter outside the health centre. We had the money set aside for it, and we'd heard that the bus company might change the route, but they've now confirmed that it will stay the same. Unfortunately, the highways department have told us that a shelter in the position we'd chosen would block drivers' view of the junction, which would be dangerous. So we'll have to find a different spot, and that will take a little longer. Councillor Hale: And finally, on Mill Street, there have been a lot of complaints about drivers going too fast, particularly at the times when children are arriving at or leaving the primary school. So we've put up signs asking drivers to slow down near the school, and we'll be monitoring the situation. Some parents asked for signs telling cyclists to get off and walk, but we don't think that's necessary at the moment. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20. Chair: Thank you. Next on the agenda is the plan for Riverside Park. Councillor Hale again. Councillor Hale: Yes. As you know, the council has recently bought some extra land next to the park, and we've been asking local people how the whole area could be improved. If you look at the plan on the screen, you'll see the river running along the top, the community hall near the entrance from Station Road, and the football pitch in the middle. Councillor Hale: At the moment, people park their cars between the community hall and the line of trees, which is dangerous because children walk through there on their way to the football pitch. So we're proposing a new car park on the other side of the community hall, right next to it, on the western edge of the park. Councillor Hale: Then there's the new land, which is on the far side of the line of trees. We plan to put two new tennis courts there, in the northern part of the new land, towards the river, where the ground is flat. The southern part of the new land will be left as a wildflower meadow. Councillor Hale: We're also going to build a small café. We did consider putting it next to the football pitch, but we think it will be more attractive by the river, so it'll be at the far end of the footpath that runs from the community hall down to the water. Councillor Hale: Another popular request was for an outdoor gym, with exercise equipment that anyone can use free of charge. We thought about putting it by the river, too, but in the end we decided it should go in the south-east corner of the park, near the road, where there's more light in the evenings. Councillor Hale: People also asked for somewhere to have picnics. So we'll be putting tables and benches beside the river, just to the west of the line of trees, where there's a lovely view along the water. Councillor Hale: And finally, there'll be a new notice board with information about events in the park. That will be directly on your right as you come into the park from the road, so that everyone will see it. Chair: Thank you, Councillor. Are there any questions? That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two hospitality students called Mia and Ben discussing their report on street food markets in different cities. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24. Mia: So, Ben, now that we've finished the research on street food markets, we need to decide how to organise the report. Ben: Right. I think we should start with the benefits. Street food markets have become so popular in the last ten years, and people often say it's because they offer cheap meals. Mia: Yes, but in a lot of the markets we looked at, the food wasn't actually that cheap. Some of it cost as much as a restaurant meal. Ben: That's true. What I think matters more is that they give people with a small business a chance to get started. Opening a restaurant costs a fortune, but anyone with a good recipe can rent a stall for a few days a week and see if people like their food. Mia: I agree. That's one of the most important points. A lot of the stallholders we read about went on to open their own restaurants. And the other really important thing is the way markets bring people together. You see families, students and office workers all sitting at the same tables. Ben: Definitely. In some cities, the markets have become the centre of the community. They attract tourists too, of course. Mia: They do, but I don't think that's the main point. Some people also claim that markets reduce food waste, because stallholders only cook what they can sell. Ben: I'm not convinced. I didn't find any real evidence for that. Mia: No, neither did I. OK, so shall we move on to our recommendations? What makes a market successful? Ben: Well, some of the newer markets have live music every evening, which is nice, but I wouldn't say it's essential. Mia: No. But what is essential is clear rules on hygiene. If people get ill after eating at a market, the news spreads very quickly, and the whole market suffers, not just the stall concerned. Ben: Absolutely. And the fees that stallholders pay for their pitch need to be kept low. The markets where the fees went up too quickly lost their best traders, because small businesses simply couldn't afford to stay. Mia: Good point. Some people argue that a market should be run by a single company, but actually some of the most successful ones are run by a group of traders together. And covered seating is useful, but plenty of markets manage without it. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30. Ben: Right, shall we go through the examples now and say what we think of each one? Mia: OK. Let's start with Copenhagen. The street food market there is in an old industrial building by the harbour. Ben: I really didn't expect it to do well. It's quite a long way from the city centre, and for much of the year the weather's cold and windy. But it's packed most evenings, and the visitor numbers keep growing. Mia: I know. I was amazed by the visitor numbers too. I think the old building gives it a special atmosphere, but even so, I wouldn't have predicted it. Next, Bangkok. Street food is a huge part of life there. Ben: I think it's successful mainly because the food is so cheap that people eat out almost every day. Mia: I'm not sure about that. I'd say it's more about the variety. You can find food from every region of the country on one street. Ben: Well, we'll have to agree to differ. What about Mexico City? Mia: The food's wonderful, but a lot of the stalls don't have proper seating, and many of them don't have running water for washing their hands and equipment. Ben: Yes, and I read that the stallholders themselves have been asking the city for better facilities. That's definitely what's needed. Mia: Agreed. Then Singapore, with its hawker centres. Ben: They're amazing. Every stall has a hygiene grade displayed, the centres are cleaned every day, and there are clear rules about everything from rubbish to prices. Some people say they've expanded too fast, but I think they've been carefully planned. Mia: I agree. It's an excellent system. What about London? We looked at the market near London Bridge. Ben: The food is excellent, and the atmosphere is great, but I found the prices shocking. I don't think many local people could afford to eat there regularly. Mia: That's what I thought too. It seems to be mainly for tourists and people with well-paid jobs nearby. Some of the stallholders told a newspaper that they'd had to raise their prices because the rent for their pitch had gone up so much. Ben: And finally, Taipei, with its night markets. Mia: They're still very popular, but some of the famous ones seem to have changed a lot. They used to be places where local families went for dinner, but now a lot of the stalls sell the same snacks to tourists. Ben: Yes, I got that impression too. They're not quite what they used to be. OK, I think we've got enough to start writing. That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear part of an environmental science lecture about an animal called the thylacine, which is now extinct. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Lecturer: Today I'd like to look at one of the best-known extinctions of the twentieth century, that of the thylacine, which is often called the Tasmanian tiger. Despite its name, it wasn't related to tigers at all. It was a marsupial, the largest meat-eating marsupial of modern times, and its closest living relatives are small animals such as the numbat. It's a story that shows how quickly a species can disappear, even one that had survived in one form or another for millions of years. Lecturer: Thousands of years ago, the thylacine was found across mainland Australia and New Guinea. But it disappeared from the mainland around three thousand years ago, probably because of competition from dingoes, which had been brought to Australia by people, and perhaps also because of hunting. By the time Europeans arrived, the only place it survived was the island of Tasmania, off the south coast. Lecturer: The first European settlers arrived in Tasmania in eighteen oh three, and before long, large areas of land were being used for farming. Many of the farmers kept sheep, and when sheep were found dead, the thylacine was very often blamed. Whether this was fair is something I'll come back to. In eighteen eighty-eight, the government began paying a bounty for every adult thylacine that was killed, and by the time the scheme ended in nineteen oh nine, more than two thousand bounties had been paid. Private companies paid rewards as well, so the true number killed was certainly higher. Lecturer: By the nineteen twenties, sightings in the wild had become very rare. The last known thylacine died in a zoo in Hobart, the capital of Tasmania, in September nineteen thirty-six. Ironically, the animal was officially protected by law only a few weeks before it died. Lecturer: So what did the thylacine look like? It was roughly the size of a medium-sized dog, and in many ways it looked like one, with a long head and a stiff tail. But it had a series of dark stripes across its lower back, which is where the name tiger came from. Like other marsupials, the female carried her young in a pouch, where they stayed for several months after birth. Lecturer: Thylacines were mostly active at night, and during the day they rested in hollow logs, among rocks or in thick vegetation. Early settlers generally described them as shy animals that avoided people, and there are very few reliable reports of them attacking humans. Lecturer: We are lucky to have more than just drawings and preserved specimens. In nineteen thirty-three, a naturalist recorded a short black and white film of one of the last captive animals, and you can still watch it today. It lasts less than a minute and a half, but it shows the animal pacing around its enclosure and opening its jaws remarkably wide. Lecturer: Now, in recent years, scientists have used modern techniques to find out more about how the thylacine lived. One study used computer models of its skull to calculate how much force it could apply when biting. The results were surprising. Although the thylacine could open its mouth very wide, its jaw was relatively weak compared with those of other predators of a similar size. Lecturer: What this suggests is that the thylacine probably hunted animals that were much smaller than itself, such as possums and bandicoots, rather than sheep, which would have been too large and too strong for it to kill easily. In other words, the farmers' belief that thylacines were a serious threat to their flocks may well have been mistaken, and many of the sheep deaths were more likely to have been caused by wild dogs. Lecturer: So why did the thylacine disappear so quickly? Hunting was clearly important, but it was probably not the only cause. In the early nineteen hundreds, there are reports of a disease, similar to one that affects dogs, which seems to have killed many thylacines both in the wild and in zoos. With numbers already reduced by hunting, the population may not have been able to recover. Lecturer: Another factor was the loss of habitat. As more and more forest and grassland was cleared for farms and settlements, the thylacine had fewer places to live and to find food. Some researchers believe that even if hunting had stopped earlier, this alone might eventually have been enough to drive the species to extinction. Lecturer: Today, the thylacine has become a symbol of Tasmania, and there are still occasional reported sightings, although none has ever been confirmed. Some scientists are even attempting to recreate the animal using its preserved genetic material, although whether this will ever be possible remains to be seen. In two thousand and seventeen, scientists announced that they had sequenced its complete genetic code, using a young thylacine that had been preserved in alcohol in a museum for more than a century. That is the end of Part 4. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear a town councillor reporting on the town centre and on plans for a local park. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14. Chair: Right, next on the agenda is the town centre. Councillor Hale. Councillor Hale: Thank you. Well, we now have the results of the survey we carried out in the spring about the town centre. To be honest, we'd expected parking to be the biggest issue, but very few people complained about it, and the new car park behind the library seems to have helped. Some people mentioned the cost of bus fares, although that isn't something the council controls. But by far the most common concern was the growing number of empty shops. People feel that the high street is starting to look neglected, and they're worried about what that means for the town. Councillor Hale: We're looking at ways of encouraging new businesses to move in, and I'll report back on that next month. In the meantime, there are some smaller changes we can make straight away. In the market square, we'll be planting a row of trees along the south side this autumn, to provide some shade and make it a more pleasant place to sit. The fountain, which many of you will remember was broken for years, was repaired last summer and is working well. There's been talk of closing the square to cars completely, but that's a longer-term idea and it would need a lot more consultation. Councillor Hale: Now, you'll remember that we planned to put up a new bus shelter outside the health centre. We had the money set aside for it, and we'd heard that the bus company might change the route, but they've now confirmed that it will stay the same. Unfortunately, the highways department have told us that a shelter in the position we'd chosen would block drivers' view of the junction, which would be dangerous. So we'll have to find a different spot, and that will take a little longer. Councillor Hale: And finally, on Mill Street, there have been a lot of complaints about drivers going too fast, particularly at the times when children are arriving at or leaving the primary school. So we've put up signs asking drivers to slow down near the school, and we'll be monitoring the situation. Some parents asked for signs telling cyclists to get off and walk, but we don't think that's necessary at the moment. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20. Chair: Thank you. Next on the agenda is the plan for Riverside Park. Councillor Hale again. Councillor Hale: Yes. As you know, the council has recently bought some extra land next to the park, and we've been asking local people how the whole area could be improved. If you look at the plan on the screen, you'll see the river running along the top, the community hall near the entrance from Station Road, and the football pitch in the middle. Councillor Hale: At the moment, people park their cars between the community hall and the line of trees, which is dangerous because children walk through there on their way to the football pitch. So we're proposing a new car park on the other side of the community hall, right next to it, on the western edge of the park. Councillor Hale: Then there's the new land, which is on the far side of the line of trees. We plan to put two new tennis courts there, in the northern part of the new land, towards the river, where the ground is flat. The southern part of the new land will be left as a wildflower meadow. Councillor Hale: We're also going to build a small café. We did consider putting it next to the football pitch, but we think it will be more attractive by the river, so it'll be at the far end of the footpath that runs from the community hall down to the water. Councillor Hale: Another popular request was for an outdoor gym, with exercise equipment that anyone can use free of charge. We thought about putting it by the river, too, but in the end we decided it should go in the south-east corner of the park, near the road, where there's more light in the evenings. Councillor Hale: People also asked for somewhere to have picnics. So we'll be putting tables and benches beside the river, just to the west of the line of trees, where there's a lovely view along the water. Councillor Hale: And finally, there'll be a new notice board with information about events in the park. That will be directly on your right as you come into the park from the road, so that everyone will see it. Chair: Thank you, Councillor. Are there any questions? That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two hospitality students called Mia and Ben discussing their report on street food markets in different cities. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24. Mia: So, Ben, now that we've finished the research on street food markets, we need to decide how to organise the report. Ben: Right. I think we should start with the benefits. Street food markets have become so popular in the last ten years, and people often say it's because they offer cheap meals. Mia: Yes, but in a lot of the markets we looked at, the food wasn't actually that cheap. Some of it cost as much as a restaurant meal. Ben: That's true. What I think matters more is that they give people with a small business a chance to get started. Opening a restaurant costs a fortune, but anyone with a good recipe can rent a stall for a few days a week and see if people like their food. Mia: I agree. That's one of the most important points. A lot of the stallholders we read about went on to open their own restaurants. And the other really important thing is the way markets bring people together. You see families, students and office workers all sitting at the same tables. Ben: Definitely. In some cities, the markets have become the centre of the community. They attract tourists too, of course. Mia: They do, but I don't think that's the main point. Some people also claim that markets reduce food waste, because stallholders only cook what they can sell. Ben: I'm not convinced. I didn't find any real evidence for that. Mia: No, neither did I. OK, so shall we move on to our recommendations? What makes a market successful? Ben: Well, some of the newer markets have live music every evening, which is nice, but I wouldn't say it's essential. Mia: No. But what is essential is clear rules on hygiene. If people get ill after eating at a market, the news spreads very quickly, and the whole market suffers, not just the stall concerned. Ben: Absolutely. And the fees that stallholders pay for their pitch need to be kept low. The markets where the fees went up too quickly lost their best traders, because small businesses simply couldn't afford to stay. Mia: Good point. Some people argue that a market should be run by a single company, but actually some of the most successful ones are run by a group of traders together. And covered seating is useful, but plenty of markets manage without it. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30. Ben: Right, shall we go through the examples now and say what we think of each one? Mia: OK. Let's start with Copenhagen. The street food market there is in an old industrial building by the harbour. Ben: I really didn't expect it to do well. It's quite a long way from the city centre, and for much of the year the weather's cold and windy. But it's packed most evenings, and the visitor numbers keep growing. Mia: I know. I was amazed by the visitor numbers too. I think the old building gives it a special atmosphere, but even so, I wouldn't have predicted it. Next, Bangkok. Street food is a huge part of life there. Ben: I think it's successful mainly because the food is so cheap that people eat out almost every day. Mia: I'm not sure about that. I'd say it's more about the variety. You can find food from every region of the country on one street. Ben: Well, we'll have to agree to differ. What about Mexico City? Mia: The food's wonderful, but a lot of the stalls don't have proper seating, and many of them don't have running water for washing their hands and equipment. Ben: Yes, and I read that the stallholders themselves have been asking the city for better facilities. That's definitely what's needed. Mia: Agreed. Then Singapore, with its hawker centres. Ben: They're amazing. Every stall has a hygiene grade displayed, the centres are cleaned every day, and there are clear rules about everything from rubbish to prices. Some people say they've expanded too fast, but I think they've been carefully planned. Mia: I agree. It's an excellent system. What about London? We looked at the market near London Bridge. Ben: The food is excellent, and the atmosphere is great, but I found the prices shocking. I don't think many local people could afford to eat there regularly. Mia: That's what I thought too. It seems to be mainly for tourists and people with well-paid jobs nearby. Some of the stallholders told a newspaper that they'd had to raise their prices because the rent for their pitch had gone up so much. Ben: And finally, Taipei, with its night markets. Mia: They're still very popular, but some of the famous ones seem to have changed a lot. They used to be places where local families went for dinner, but now a lot of the stalls sell the same snacks to tourists. Ben: Yes, I got that impression too. They're not quite what they used to be. OK, I think we've got enough to start writing. That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear part of an environmental science lecture about an animal called the thylacine, which is now extinct. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Lecturer: Today I'd like to look at one of the best-known extinctions of the twentieth century, that of the thylacine, which is often called the Tasmanian tiger. Despite its name, it wasn't related to tigers at all. It was a marsupial, the largest meat-eating marsupial of modern times, and its closest living relatives are small animals such as the numbat. It's a story that shows how quickly a species can disappear, even one that had survived in one form or another for millions of years. Lecturer: Thousands of years ago, the thylacine was found across mainland Australia and New Guinea. But it disappeared from the mainland around three thousand years ago, probably because of competition from dingoes, which had been brought to Australia by people, and perhaps also because of hunting. By the time Europeans arrived, the only place it survived was the island of Tasmania, off the south coast. Lecturer: The first European settlers arrived in Tasmania in eighteen oh three, and before long, large areas of land were being used for farming. Many of the farmers kept sheep, and when sheep were found dead, the thylacine was very often blamed. Whether this was fair is something I'll come back to. In eighteen eighty-eight, the government began paying a bounty for every adult thylacine that was killed, and by the time the scheme ended in nineteen oh nine, more than two thousand bounties had been paid. Private companies paid rewards as well, so the true number killed was certainly higher. Lecturer: By the nineteen twenties, sightings in the wild had become very rare. The last known thylacine died in a zoo in Hobart, the capital of Tasmania, in September nineteen thirty-six. Ironically, the animal was officially protected by law only a few weeks before it died. Lecturer: So what did the thylacine look like? It was roughly the size of a medium-sized dog, and in many ways it looked like one, with a long head and a stiff tail. But it had a series of dark stripes across its lower back, which is where the name tiger came from. Like other marsupials, the female carried her young in a pouch, where they stayed for several months after birth. Lecturer: Thylacines were mostly active at night, and during the day they rested in hollow logs, among rocks or in thick vegetation. Early settlers generally described them as shy animals that avoided people, and there are very few reliable reports of them attacking humans. Lecturer: We are lucky to have more than just drawings and preserved specimens. In nineteen thirty-three, a naturalist recorded a short black and white film of one of the last captive animals, and you can still watch it today. It lasts less than a minute and a half, but it shows the animal pacing around its enclosure and opening its jaws remarkably wide. Lecturer: Now, in recent years, scientists have used modern techniques to find out more about how the thylacine lived. One study used computer models of its skull to calculate how much force it could apply when biting. The results were surprising. Although the thylacine could open its mouth very wide, its jaw was relatively weak compared with those of other predators of a similar size. Lecturer: What this suggests is that the thylacine probably hunted animals that were much smaller than itself, such as possums and bandicoots, rather than sheep, which would have been too large and too strong for it to kill easily. In other words, the farmers' belief that thylacines were a serious threat to their flocks may well have been mistaken, and many of the sheep deaths were more likely to have been caused by wild dogs. Lecturer: So why did the thylacine disappear so quickly? Hunting was clearly important, but it was probably not the only cause. In the early nineteen hundreds, there are reports of a disease, similar to one that affects dogs, which seems to have killed many thylacines both in the wild and in zoos. With numbers already reduced by hunting, the population may not have been able to recover. Lecturer: Another factor was the loss of habitat. As more and more forest and grassland was cleared for farms and settlements, the thylacine had fewer places to live and to find food. Some researchers believe that even if hunting had stopped earlier, this alone might eventually have been enough to drive the species to extinction. Lecturer: Today, the thylacine has become a symbol of Tasmania, and there are still occasional reported sightings, although none has ever been confirmed. Some scientists are even attempting to recreate the animal using its preserved genetic material, although whether this will ever be possible remains to be seen. In two thousand and seventeen, scientists announced that they had sequenced its complete genetic code, using a young thylacine that had been preserved in alcohol in a museum for more than a century. That is the end of Part 4. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.
